name: @fjellrute/mobile
//: Phases 2 and 3 of Fjellrute-Mobile-Build-Plan.docx: the Expo app. It shares packages/core with apps/web — geometry, the saved-routes client, the i18n store, the Kartverket and NVE layer descriptors — so there is exactly one definition of each and no drift between phone and laptop.
//versions: The four pinned versions below are not guesses: they were read off a working SDK 57 scaffold produced by create-expo-app on 2026-08-25 (spikes/webview-3d/app). Everything Expo manages on top of them — expo-router, expo-secure-store, expo-location, the MapLibre native module — is installed by ./setup.sh through `expo install`, which resolves the version each package must have for THIS SDK. That indirection is deliberate. Hand-written version ranges for native modules are how you get a build that compiles and then crashes on the device, and this project has already lost an evening to an Expo version that was inferred rather than read.
//nativeModules: Five of the six react-native-* entries in `dependencies` are there despite nothing in app/ or src/ importing them — react-native-svg is the exception and has its own note below. expo-router and @expo/ui declare them as PEER dependencies, and pnpm installs missing peers automatically — resolving each to the newest version satisfying the peer's own range, which is not the version Expo pinned for this SDK. Undeclared, they were invisible to `expo install --fix`, which audits package.json and therefore reported everything up to date while the tree held worklets 0.12.1 against Expo's 0.10.1. Native autolinking does not care that no JavaScript imports them: expo-modules-core compiles C++ against react-native-worklets' headers, and 0.12.1 had dropped the WorkletRuntime::executeSync that it calls, so the Android build failed in the C++ compiler. Declaring them at the versions in expo/bundledNativeModules.json is what makes the resolution explicit rather than emergent; the root package.json also overrides three of them so a second copy cannot exist for autolinking to find. Change them only to match bundledNativeModules.json — scripts/verify-mobile-app.mjs compares the two. THIS COMMENT LIVES AT THE TOP LEVEL, not next to the entries it describes, because pnpm reads a `//`-prefixed key inside `dependencies` as a package name and fails the whole install with ERR_PNPM_INVALID_PACKAGE_NAME. The root manifest says so too, and this file broke anyway; scripts/verify-mobile-app.mjs now enforces it.
//react-native-svg: Added by Phase 2 of docs/mobile-web-parity-plan.md, for the elevation profile. The plan named it and named why: the profile is the highest-value thing on the phone's route screen, computeProfile already exists in packages/core so there is no logic left to write, and the only missing piece was something to draw a few hundred coloured line segments with. Recharts is out — it renders DOM. react-native-svg is the low-risk choice because apps/web already draws this exact chart by hand in SVG for the printed briefing (briefing/ProfileSvg.tsx), so the drawing carries over almost element for element, and because the same primitives cover Phase 3's snow chart when it arrives. It IS a native module, at the version in expo/bundledNativeModules.json like every other one here, which means the existing development build on your device does not contain it: `npx expo run:android` (or a fresh `eas build --profile development`) once, before `pnpm start` will show you anything but a redbox about RNSVGSvgView. That rebuild is the whole cost of this dependency and it is a one-off.
//phase4-drawing: Phase 4 of docs/mobile-web-parity-plan.md — touch drawing and erasing on the planner map — added NO dependency at all, native or otherwise, and therefore needs NO rebuild: the development build you already have on the device runs it after nothing more than `pnpm start`. That is worth stating explicitly, because it was not the obvious outcome. The obvious gesture library is react-native-gesture-handler, which is already in `dependencies` above (expo-router's peer, listed for the autolinking reasons in //nativeModules) — but using it needs a GestureHandlerRootView wrapped around app/_layout.tsx, which changes touch delivery for every screen in the app, and its Android path needs the native module actually linked, which no one here can verify without a device build. src/ui/DrawingSurface.tsx uses React Native's own PanResponder instead: no provider, no native module, and the per-touch work is a subtraction and a comparison. The maths it feeds — RDP simplification, the disk eraser, the synchronous Mercator projection the map's own async project() cannot provide — all lives in packages/core, where the plan's one rule says it belongs, so there was nothing left for a native module to do. If strokes ever feel laggy on a real phone, react-native-gesture-handler is the upgrade, and it costs a rebuild at that point.
//saved-routes-row-actions: The saved-routes list gained the web's four row actions, and three of them needed something the phone did not have. expo-clipboard backs `copy public link`; expo-file-system writes the GPX that packages/core's routeToGpx already produces as a string; expo-sharing hands that file to the OS share sheet, which is the phone's equivalent of the browser's download — there is no downloads folder to drop it in. All three are NATIVE modules, at the versions in expo/bundledNativeModules.json like every other one here, so the development build on your device does not contain them: `npx expo run:android` (or a fresh `eas build --profile development`) once, before `pnpm start` will show anything but a redbox. One rebuild covers all three. Nothing else in this phase adds a dependency.

scripts.//web: There is deliberately no `web` script. `expo start --web` cannot run this app: MapLibre React Native has no web renderer, and expo-secure-store has no web implementation, so there is nowhere for the session to live. A script that is guaranteed to fail is worse than no script — it reads as a supported path.
scripts.//typecheck: Not wired into the root `pnpm build`. That runs `tsc -b` over the project references in the root tsconfig.json, where packages/core is compiled with `types: []` to keep it platform-free; adding this app there would put React Native's types into the same solution and the boundary harness would lose its meaning. Run it from here instead.
